title: Power Automate
note: Power Automate reduced to fit and governance: which tool for which job, environments and data policies, ALM and ownership, and licensing as a design constraint. Limits and licenses are as of Nov 2026; flow-building detail lives in Microsoft Learn. Refresh quarterly.

concepts.s: Use Power Automate for Microsoft 365 workflow, approvals and light integration, an enterprise iPaaS like Workato for cross-SaaS integration and APIs, and Fabric or Databricks for data movement.

x.b:
• Power Automate: approvals, notifications, SharePoint, Teams, Outlook and Dataverse logic, desktop RPA, flows called by Copilot Studio agents.
  • Logic Apps: same expression language, Azure-managed deployment and monitoring, for IT-built integration.
  • Workato: cross-SaaS integration, APIs, governed agent tools.
  • Fabric Data Factory or Databricks: scheduled and bulk data movement and transformation.
Trap: Moving data in flows row by row: every action is a metered request and loops multiply them.
A manager approval for access requests: Power Automate. Syncing 2M claims nightly: Fabric or Databricks.

cards.q: A team wants a flow to copy 2M rows nightly into the lakehouse. Better tool?
cards.a: Fabric Data Factory or Databricks: bulk data movement isn't Power Automate's job.

cards.q: Where does Power Automate clearly win?
cards.a: Microsoft 365-centric workflow: approvals, Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, Dataverse and Power Apps logic.

concepts.s: Environments are the security and deployment boundary, and data policies decide which connectors, actions and endpoints flows may use, so PHI flows live in governed environments with deny-by-default policies.

x.b:
• Each environment has its own Dataverse, roles and connections; Managed Environments add sharing limits, usage insights, pipelines and more.
  • Classic data policies group connectors as Business, Non-business or Blocked; a flow can't mix the first two. Action control and endpoint filtering narrow further.
  • Advanced connector policies (GA June 2026) are default-deny allowlists assigned to an environment or an environment group (groups need Managed Environments).
Trap: Building production flows in the default environment, where every licensed user is a maker.
A PHI environment group allows only Dataverse, SharePoint and approved SQL endpoints; everything else is blocked.

cards.q: A flow combining a Business and a Non-business connector won't save. Why?
cards.a: Classic data policies forbid mixing those groups in one flow.

cards.q: Why avoid the default environment for production flows?
cards.a: Every licensed user can build there, so governance and isolation are weak.

concepts.s: Build in solutions, externalize settings as environment variables and connection references, promote managed solutions through pipelines, and let a service principal or group own production flows.

x.b:
• Unmanaged solutions in dev; managed solutions in test and prod.
  • Environment variables and connection references swap per environment; only solution flows support them.
  • Pipelines in Power Platform deploy to Managed Environments, with delegated deployment so makers never need production rights. Git integration syncs development environments' solutions to source control.
  • Flows owned by a person stop working when that person leaves; a service principal can own solution flows (premium ones need a Process license).
Trap: Production flows owned by an individual's account: they break on departure or license change.
A pipeline promotes the approvals solution from dev to prod as a service principal; prod connection references point at the prod SharePoint site.

cards.q: A critical flow stopped when its maker left. What prevents this?
cards.a: Service principal ownership of the solution flow; group co-owners only add editors, the flow still runs on the owner's license and connections.

cards.q: What lets one solution point at dev resources in dev and prod resources in prod?

concepts.s: Every trigger and action is a metered request, so the license behind a flow sets its daily allowance and burst limits, and loop design drives cost and throttling.

x.b:
• Official allocations: Premium 40,000 actions per user per day, Process 250,000 per flow or bot (stackable), Microsoft 365 seeded 6,000 with standard connectors only. As of Nov 2026 a transition period applies higher per-flow limits; per-user pooling phases in from April 2027.
  • Burst limit: 100,000 requests in any rolling five minutes.
  • Failed actions, retries, pagination and every loop iteration count; skipped actions don't.
  • Multiplexing: every user who triggers a premium flow, directly or indirectly, needs Premium, or the flow needs Process; automated flows run on the owner's license, and people who only receive output aren't multiplexing.
Trap: A loop over 10,000 rows with 5 actions each: 50,000 requests in one run.
Replace an apply-to-each with Select and Filter array, which reshape whole arrays in one request each.

cards.q: A flow throttles during month-end. What design change helps most?
cards.a: Cut requests: filter at the source and replace loops with Select and Filter array.

cards.q: Thirty colleagues trigger a premium instant flow. What licensing applies?
cards.a: Each triggering user needs Premium, or the flow gets a Process license.

concepts.s: Filter at the trigger, guard against self-retriggering, wrap work in Try and Catch scopes that end Failed, and make every write safe to rerun.

x.b:
• Trigger conditions (@expressions) stop unwanted runs before they start; add a loop guard (or, on Dataverse, Select columns) so the flow's own writes don't retrigger it.
  • Try / Catch / Finally scopes via configure run after; Catch sets a flag, and a Terminate (Failed) after Finally fires on it, since Terminate skips everything after it.
  • Idempotency: upsert on a key, mark processed rows, build idempotency keys from stable fields (never guid()).
  • Child flows split big flows; put irreversible trigger concurrency on a small child.

Trap: Retrying a non-idempotent POST with the default retry policy: a timeout after commit creates duplicates.
Trap: Turning on trigger concurrency casually: it can't be turned off; you rebuild the flow.
A Dataverse flow syncs contacts to the EHR and writes back a sync timestamp. Its trigger's Select columns lists only fields users edit, so the write-back can't retrigger it.

cards.q: A flow updates the row that triggers it and runs until throttled. Fix?
cards.a: Stop its own writes firing it: a trigger-condition loop guard or, on Dataverse, Select columns.

cards.q: A Catch scope sends an email and the run shows Succeeded. What's missing?
cards.a: A Terminate with status Failed, placed after Finally and run only when Catch ran.
